1:
Gill limits the first outcry to the princes and elders standing by when the report was delivered, though word would soon spread and raise a general clamour. Henry lays the mischief at the door of the ten, supposing the twelve had talked the matter over before reporting, and that Caleb and Joshua did their utmost to bring the rest round — had the others but let Caleb speak for them all, nothing would have come of it; instead the ten seem to have designed the mutiny deliberately, against Moses and Aaron, though they could propose no gain unless they hoped to command the retreat. Calvin sees it from the other end, how easily a few incentives raise sedition in a multitude, which left to itself is like a sea open to every tempest. He grants a pretext, ten chosen men dissuading and only two advising, but will not excuse the credulity, since it grew out of incredulity: if the standing of ten men weighed so much, how much more the word of God, who had promised that land four centuries before. Clarke draws a character instead: with scarcely any firmness of mind and almost no religion they bore no reverse and were forever at their wit's end, headstrong and pusillanimous by turns — and because they were such, the power and wisdom of God stand out the more in their story.

The wish to have died already Henry treats as causeless discontent. Never had months been spent so pleasantly as those since Egypt, loaded with honours and favours, yet they would rather have perished with the firstborn or with those lately struck down for lusting — choosing to die criminals under God's justice than live conquerors in his favour. It is unbridled passion, he says, that makes men prodigal of the one thing nature holds dearest; they wish to die for fear of dying, without the sense of the lepers who reasoned that if their enemies killed them they should but die. He notes that some render the words as a present wish, and Calvin argues the point against the old interpreter, who took the optative particle for a negative and made them say their death in the wilderness would be bitterer than in Egypt — whereas their complaint is of the death they expect ahead. Wesley adds the grim sequel, that they had their wish before long and did die in that wilderness.

From the men to their Master is a short step, and all mark it. Wesley says that from the instruments they rise higher and strike at God, the author of the journey, which shows how fast sin grows unresisted; and Ellicott that the revolt is now open against Jehovah himself, to whom they impute the exodus by way of reproach. Ellicott would render the question as a present one, wherefore doth the Lord bring us into this land, and identifies the danger they feared as the sword of the Amorite and the Anakim rather than famine. Keil calls it a murmuring growing into open revolt. Calvin is harshest on the charge itself: they accuse God of deception and cruelty, as if he were betraying them to the Canaanites, and of weakness besides — repaying his kindnesses by calling him their betrayer. On the proposed election Gill notes that they had captains over the tribes and wanted one commander over all, and that Nehemiah speaks as if the appointment was made, their will being taken for the deed; Clarke calls it a formal renunciation of Moses and flat rebellion, and marvels that men whose lives had been embittered by Egyptian rigour should be eager to return, past evils weighing less than present ones far smaller. Wesley presses the folly — who would cover them with a cloud, feed them with manna, bring them over the sea, or answer for their welcome among the Egyptians they had ruined?
5:
What the prostration meant is disputed. Gill offers three readings — shame at so shocking a proposal, an appeal to the people to lay the thought aside, or a supplication that God would convince them of their folly. Henry takes it as all three at once, and adds a practical reason: the noise was such that they could not be heard, and calling for silence would have made the crowd louder, so they gained a hearing by falling down in sight of the assembly — praying God to still the noise of that sea, showing the trouble of their own spirits as men astonished to see a people fling away their mercies. Calvin doubts whether they humbled themselves before the people or fell in prayer, and prefers the second, as a rebuke of their stupidity by turning to God — for in such obduracy nothing was left but to call on him, yet openly, since a retired place would have served had prayer alone been the point. Wesley reads it as the refuge Moses always took in such straits, done before all the assembly that the sight might awaken them.

The rending of garments Calvin explains as an eastern usage, solemn in extreme grief or in abhorrence of a crime, which hypocrites afterwards imitated to feign sorrow or deceive the simple — though here it was genuine; and he observes that Joshua's courage is now named where before only Caleb was praised. Wesley refers it to grief at the blasphemy and sedition and the judgment they foresaw; Henry adds that their share in the commission made the tumult theirs, their colleagues having raised the storm. On the plea Henry admires the reasoning: they commend the land as very, very good, so the word runs, giving no ground to despise so pleasant a place — men convinced of the gains of religion would not stick at its services. Calvin fastens on the conditional particle. Some take it as causal, that because God loves us he will bring us in, which he rejects as foreign to the sense; the doubt is put in not to weaken hope but to bring them to repent, and the words only rebel not show that nothing shuts up God's way but their own refusal to obey.

The plea turns on two figures. Henry makes light of the walled cities: though the Canaanites are fortified they are naked, that common providence which guards the rights of nations having abandoned them — no people can be safe when they have provoked God to leave them — while Israel, though in tents, is fortified, the Lord being there and his name a strong tower. Clarke and Ellicott note that the defence departed is literally a shadow, a figure of force in hot countries where shelter from the sun is worth much; Clarke adds that Arabs and Persians use the same word, while Ellicott holds the iniquity of the Canaanites now full and themselves ripe for destruction. Wesley turns the other figure practically — we shall destroy them as easily as we eat bread — and warns that nothing can ruin sinners but their own rebellion, since if God leaves them it is because they drive him away. On the sentence of stoning Gill and Ellicott agree that the congregation must mean the princes and chief men, there being otherwise nobody to address the order to; Ellicott adds that Moses had feared the same violence before. Calvin is unsurprised: men who have censured God will rage against his servants, reproof of iniquity ending at last in fury; and God does not argue or threaten but displays his power, rescuing them as from wild beasts. Clarke draws the moral that a man is immortal till his work is done, and Ellicott places the appearing in the court rather than the tent, since the people could not otherwise have seen it.
11:
Henry reads the summons as a vindication: while the people were busy disgracing Moses, God called him to the tabernacle and put public honour on him as the man of his counsel. Two things are complained of. The first is the sin, and Henry gives the word its range, that they provoke, or reject, reproach and despise, because they will not believe; unbelief is the bitter root, distrust of God's power being itself a great provocation and lying at the bottom of many others. The second is persistence: heaven keeps account of how long men hold out, and the longer they hold the greater the offence. He finds two aggravations — that they were a peculiar and professing people, the nearer to God in name the more provoking their sins, and that they had seen every sign shown among them. Calvin fixes on the same obstinacy, that they had rejected God with atrocious insults in the face of the clearest proofs of his power. He is unsure of the verb, doubting the rendering provoke and thinking Jerome nearer with how long will they detract me, but rests on the plain drift, which the next clause confirms: God complains of being disparaged, since they will not weigh the miracles that testified his power and kindness, refusing credit to a heap of signs that ought to have broken their stubbornness. The words how long, he adds, measure both the length of the crime and the patience of God.

The sentence Henry states without softening: what remains but to make a full end, smite them with pestilence, blot out name and race, and so be eased of his adversaries — they wished to die, and they may die. If it is asked what becomes of the covenant with Abraham, the answer stands in the same breath: it will be kept in the family of Moses, of whom a greater nation shall be made. Henry takes this for a trial: God would see whether Moses still preferred Israel's interest to the advancement of his own house, and it appears he was of the same public spirit and could not bear to raise his name upon the ruin of theirs. Ellicott notes that the same promise was made at the rebellion at Sinai, and that Moses interceded then in the same way.

Whether the threat was meant to stand they answer together, and none thinks it absolute. Gill observes that the pestilence did fall, but on the spies who brought the evil report, and holds that as to the body of the people the words are partly a proposal to draw Moses out, partly a threatening to bring the nation to a sense of its sin. Wesley calls it not a determination but a commination, of the same kind as the sentence on Nineveh, with a condition implied — unless there be speedy repentance or powerful intercession. Calvin meets the difficulty head on: it may offend that God should pronounce the people cast off when their pardon was already decreed, but he is not speaking of his secret counsel, only of what they deserved and of the vengeance hanging over them, his design being never to keep Moses from praying but to prove the fervour of his zeal. Yet Calvin will not let the comfort run far, adding that though God is placable by nature, the hope of pardon is justly cut off from men so obdurate that neither his hand nor his word makes any impression. Henry turns to what followed: the sin had made a fatal breach in their defence, through which destruction would have entered had Moses not stepped in — and here he was a type of Christ, who prayed for his persecutors. The petition is one word, Pardon; and since the pardon of a national sin consists in turning away the national punishment, that is what Moses is earnest for.
13:
Gill notes that the plea begins abruptly, Moses being greatly disturbed by the threatening. Calvin has him stand in the breach of the wall, as the psalm says, resting his whole request on one thing, that God's holy name would become the sport of the wicked if the nation perished. He paraphrases: Egypt will hear, since it is notorious that this people was rescued from them by thy might; the report will pass to the Canaanites, who already know thee for their protector; and if they perish now, every nation that has heard thy fame will conclude that thy power broke down in mid course, unable to finish what it began — nothing else would occur to the heathen but that God could not maintain his own blessing. From this he draws a caution: the tie serves us only if we plead it sincerely, since many boldly urge God's name on their own behalf who care nothing for it, and the more signal his past power the more insolent the blasphemy if it seems to fail. Clarke, who thinks the passage needs no explanation, calls the arguments pointed, cogent and respectful, showing a heart full of humanity and the deepest concern for the divine glory.

What the petition for great power asks is read three ways. Gill offers two: either that the power shown in the exodus and the wilderness might appear greater still in bringing them into the promised land, or else that there might be a great display of pardoning grace — for as God's power appears in his forbearance towards the wicked, much more in forgiving them, there being more virtue in grace to pardon than in sin to damn. Wesley allows only the second, the words that follow restraining it: pardon is the single instance described in the divine titles, asked by Moses, and granted in the answer — nor is it strange that pardon should be called an act of power, being an act of omnipotent goodness. Calvin looks past the phrase to its source, that Moses draws his confidence from the vision in which God had declared his own nature. From that he takes a general rule: nothing in prayer is more effectual than to set God's word before him and build the request on his promises, as though he had dictated what we should ask; and this is why he speaks at all, to give us grounds for addressing him, since otherwise we must be dumb.

The recital of the titles raises a difficulty of its own. Wesley asks why Moses should quote the clause about visiting iniquity on the children, which looks like an argument for destroying rather than sparing. One answer is that he would not sever what God had joined; the truer answer, he thinks, is that the words should be rendered otherwise — that in destroying he will not utterly destroy, though he visit the iniquity of the fathers on the children. Gill takes the longsuffering as reaching all men and especially God's own; Calvin passes the verse by, referring his reader elsewhere. On the closing petition, however, he is full. Moses sets before himself the greatness of God's mercy and then the past proofs that he is inclined to forgive; for though iniquities heaped on iniquities might justly frighten us, the abundance of grace should swallow up all dread of wrath, as David showed when he took that refuge. Because a bare acknowledgment of God's goodness is often not enough, Moses adds the stay of experience — pardon, as thou hast so often pardoned already. Since that goodness is inexhaustible, the oftener we have proved it the more we should be emboldened to ask; not that we may indulge in sin, but that despair should not overwhelm us under condemnation. Calvin makes this the most effective importunity of all, to beseech God by benefits already received.
20:
How far the pardon reached is the question. Gill, Clarke and Wesley agree on the plain sense, that the nation was not utterly cut off; Gill reports the Jerusalem Targum's reading that the Word of the Lord remitted and forgave, which he refers to Christ, since none but God can forgive sin. Henry makes the answer a testimony to prayer: God had designed a pardon, but Moses is to have the praise of obtaining it, a whole nation rescued by one man's importunity — Pardon, says Moses; I have pardoned, says God. Ellicott balances both: justice required the transgressors to be overtaken, yet the prayer was heard and the people not exterminated. Calvin asks how God can spare men whom he determined to punish to the utmost and did shut out of their inheritance. The pardon, he answers, was granted not to the individuals but to their race and name; and rejects as unnatural the opinion that the men themselves were released from eternal death because God was satisfied with a temporal penalty. Moses was heard so far and no further, that Abraham's seed should not perish and the covenant not fail.

God swears, Gill notes, by his own life, having no greater. What the glory filling the earth means divides them. Henry hears an answer to the thing Moses had pleaded for: all the world shall see how God hates sin even in his own people and how gracious he is — as when our Saviour prayed, Father glorify thy name, and was answered that it had been glorified and should be again; those who sincerely seek God's glory may be sure of what they seek. Clarke narrows the phrase to the land: all this land, that is Canaan, fulfilled to the letter only when the preaching of Christ and his apostles was heard through all the cities of Judea, the globe not seeming to be meant wherever the expression occurs. Wesley narrows it differently, to the report of God's righteous acts in punishing this people. Calvin notes that some render the clause in the past tense, of a glory already displayed in many miracles, which chimes with the next words about men who have seen that glory; but he prefers the future, God calling to witness the glory he is about to assert — Moses having feared that the nation's ruin would become a reproach, and God now swearing to vindicate his name so that the guilty shall not go unpunished.

Whether the ten temptings are to be counted they answer three ways. Henry counts them, reckoning this exactly the tenth occasion on which the congregation had provoked God — the Red Sea, Marah, the wilderness of Sin, Rephidim, the calf, Taberah and Kibroth-hattaavah — remarking that heaven keeps a tally. Ellicott reports a like reckoning, making up the ten by adding two transgressions over the manna to the eight recorded murmurings, but thinks it likelier that ten stands, as elsewhere, for a full measure. Calvin will have no counting: the number is not fixed, and God means only that they provoked him without measure or end. He also defines the offence: to tempt God is to subject his power to the narrow rule of our senses and prescribe how he shall act to suit our desires, the root being a refusal to listen to his voice, since nothing but obedience restrains our insolence. Ellicott identifies who fell under the sentence: those numbered in the first census, Joshua and Caleb and all under twenty excepted, and any others belonging to Levi, neither numbered then nor represented among the spies. Keil explains Caleb's exemption: another spirit was in him, not the unbelieving yet proud temper of the mass but obedience and trust, so that he fulfilled to walk behind Jehovah with unwavering fidelity, and for that the land he had walked over was promised to him and his seed.
22:
Why Caleb alone is named, when Joshua stood with him, is answered three ways. Gill offers two guesses — that Joshua had no children, so nothing could be said of his seed possessing the land, or that as commander he needed no separate mention. Wesley reckons him not among the people at all, an attendant on Moses and no more to be counted with them than Moses and Aaron. Calvin grants that Joshua shared the grace but holds Caleb specially distinguished, as the man who lifted the banner first and encouraged his colleague. On the other spirit in him they agree and differ in emphasis. Wesley makes it another temper, faithful and courageous, moved not by the cowardice ruling his brethren but by the Spirit of God; Clarke will not have it a natural boldness but the influence of heaven lifting him above earthly fears, and renders the next phrase literally, that he filled up after God; Calvin, allowing that the word is sometimes used of a mere disposition, has no doubt divine inspiration is meant, and praises a man who not only exhorted others but went forward undeterred while the world was convulsed about him.

The parenthesis about the Amalekites in the valley they find hard. Ellicott sets out the difficulty: the words may join to what precedes, so that Caleb's seed should possess the land those nations occupy, but he objects to that and to taking the clause as plain geography, which suits the hill better. The verb often means a temporary sojourn, as of Joshua's ambuscade, so he would render it that they are abiding in the valley — lying in ambush, which is Ibn Ezra's reading and gives the command its force: do not walk into the snare, but turn away. Gill takes the same view, that their home was the mountain and they had come down to sit in the valley in wait, and finds goodness in the warning of a people who had provoked him. Keil reads it as a plain reason for the order, identifies the valley with the broad Wady Murreh running into the Negeb, where the Amalekites were nomads while the Canaanites held the hills, and takes Canaanite as the general name for the Amorites. Calvin canvasses three constructions and prefers a fourth, that the words are a reproach: Israel had come to the border of the inhabited land, where the enemy might have been routed, and God now turns them out of ground they had reached.

The sentence is repeated to Aaron as well as Moses, which Calvin marks as no new matter but a driving home. He hears the opening as an angry interrogation and what follows as bitter irony: nothing was further from their wish than to wander in the desert, yet God will deal with them by their own resolution and gratify them in a sense they never meant. The lifting of the hand is itself a form of swearing, as though God were called from heaven to witness and judge; and the sharpest reproof is that their self-will should annul, so far as they were concerned, a promise he had ratified by oath. Yet Calvin notes the mercy folded into the threat, that the children they had lamented over as a prey are the very ones to be given the land. Gill reports the rabbinic reading that the evil congregation means the ten spies, whence ten make a congregation, and that the murmuring is causative — but he judges the whole people meant. Ellicott and Keil note that the sentence has no verb: Ellicott would supply pardon or forgive from the earlier prayer, Keil calls it an aposiopesis and supplies the same. Keil sets out the terms: every man numbered from twenty upward should fall there, Caleb and Joshua excepted, while the little ones would be brought in to know the land their fathers despised.
33:
The word rendered wander they take otherwise. Gill has it feed, as shepherds who never rest but move on for fresh pasture; Ellicott would render it that they shall be shepherds; and Calvin makes the shepherd a figure for a sojourner with no settled residence, quoting Hezekiah's complaint that his lodging is departed like a shepherd's tent. Gill, Ellicott and Wesley agree that the forty years run from the exodus and not from the spies' return, a year and a half having already passed, and Ellicott confirms it from the later numbering, after Aaron's death. The whoredoms Calvin explains metaphorically: God having espoused this people, by rejecting his worship they broke the vow like gadding harlots; Wesley reads the phrase as the punishment of that apostasy from a Lord who was their husband. Calvin also faces what the sentence does to the innocent: God visits the fathers' sins on the children and yet chastises nobody undeservedly, since the sons who bore another's fault were not themselves guiltless. Even so he finds mercy in the delay, God waiting till the children had the strength of manhood.

Clarke sets the two forties together: the spies searched forty days and the people wander forty years ; and let them now make a captain and go back to Egypt if they can, God having hedged them so that they could neither return nor advance. The clause about knowing God's breach of promise he calls most harsh, and reports that learned men would render it my vengeance, with the Septuagint and Vulgate behind them — the sense being that God, having promised on condition of obedience, was no longer held by a covenant they had broken, so that their exclusion showed at once its annulling and his vengeance for it. Wesley keeps the covenant language but turns it back on the people: as they first broke the compact by breaking its terms, God makes it void on his side by withholding what was promised, so that the charge of breach of promise they had brought against him is seen to lie at their own door. Ellicott looks to the word itself, which occurs elsewhere only in Job, though the cognate verb is common in this book for refusing or disallowing, and settles on rejection or alienation; Keil renders it God's turning away. Calvin finds the versions various — some make it, ye shall know whether I am false — and takes it for an ironical concession by which God reproves a pride whose aim had been to charge him with falsehood.

On the sudden death of the ten Keil sees a practical proof of the threat, a stroke from before Jehovah falling visibly on the men who raised the revolt while their two colleagues were left alive. Henry places it before the sentence was published and draws two lessons from it. God marked his displeasure against men who both sinned and made Israel sin: they had slandered the land of promise, and those greatly provoke him who misrepresent religion, painting his service as mean or unprofitable; and as ring-leaders they might expect a particular mark of wrath. The survival of the other two Henry thinks the most striking part: all twelve probably stood together, and when ten fell dead of an infectious distemper the two among them were untouched, which confirmed their testimony and confounded the men who had talked of stoning them. Calvin will not allow that the notice is recorded out of order by anticipation; Moses has finished the general sentence and now sets down the spies' particular punishment, so that God begins with them and their unnatural death becomes a presage to the rest. He presses two words: the plague, implying they did not die in the course of nature, and before the Lord, which means more than in his presence, God executing judgment as though he had ascended the tribunal.
39:
What the mourning was worth they weigh carefully. Ellicott finds from what follows that the sorrow was for the punishment the sin entailed, not godly sorrow for the sin; Wesley grants the grief but says it came too late, there being now no place for repentance, and adds that such mourning there is in hell, though the tears will not quench the flames. Calvin allows it a just cause for weeping to hear that a longsuffering they had wantonly abused would hereafter be inexorable, but sets it down as the sorrow of the world that worketh death, where the wicked weep and yet never cease to murmur, gnawing the bit with more obstinacy and rushing like untamable beasts into blind despair. No tears could redeem a temporal punishment, the one remedy being to submit and calmly undergo it. Instead they struggle proudly to shake it off, and under a pretence of submission prepare to advance, wanting their confession accepted as satisfaction.

The rising is described with the same irony. Gill has them up early, in as great a haste to possess Canaan as they had lately been to return to Egypt; Ellicott renders it towards the top of the mountain, takes the route for the one the spies had used, and observes that the closing verses imply they never reached the summit. Clarke marks the contradiction: lately they thought that with Omnipotence on their side the land could not be conquered, and now imagine that without God they can drive out its inhabitants; fallen nature runs to extremes, by turns presumptuous and desperate. Henry takes it as duty mistimed turned into sin, and wishes men were as earnest for heaven while the day of grace lasts as they will be after it. They had distrusted God's strength and now presume upon their own without it.

Moses answers by asking what the transgression is; Gill names the order they broke, to turn back toward the Red sea. Calvin hears in the reply a rejection of feigned penitence, the sinner trying every shift rather than submit. To the objection that the people had no other remedy he answers that banishment from Canaan was no disinheritance from the hope of eternal life, and that by this misdirected activity they doubled the evil. The reason given is absence: Gill cites the Targum, that the ark, the tabernacle and the cloud of glory did not move; Ellicott adds that Moses already had the word of verse twenty-five and knew the visible token would not go. Both puzzle over the enemy's position, whether they had left the valley, posted a party to hold the pass, or are different portions of the same nations. Then they presumed. Gill reports the Vulgate rendering that being darkened they went up, referred by some to understandings given over to blindness and by others to a march before daylight, and an old exposition making them go obscurely because they went without leave. Calvin denies they meant to array themselves against God; rather they hoped to appease him by offering their lives up, the zeal of the wicked being fervent when it ought to be still and dead when he commands. Their senselessness appears in leaving the ark and Moses behind and running forward like doomed men; Ellicott thinks the enemy met them before ever they gained the summit. On the name Gill follows Jarchi, that Hormah is called from this slaughter, or from the later destruction of the Canaanites and so given by anticipation, or from both; the Targum makes it no name but a word, even unto destruction. Ellicott points to the article, the Hormah, the place of the ban, and thinks a common name likelier to mark three different places than one to be meant proleptically. Wesley says only that the Canaanites here are strictly the Amorites, and that the place was so called afterwards from this slaughter.
